title: client-request-shaping-and-local-fallback-playbook-2026
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

This playbook documents practical, production-ready patterns for client-side request shaping and local fallback when calling the Redwood inference API from application servers and client SDKs. It focuses on minimizing cost and tail latency while preserving correctness and observability. The guidance is intended for SDK authors, backend engineers integrating Redwood APIs, and platform teams building resilient bridges to the Redwood runtime.

Goals

- Reduce 95th/99th percentile request latency through client-side shaping and speculative strategies.
- Lower per-token compute cost via token-aware batching and prefix caching.
- Provide robust local fallback behavior to keep user-facing flows available when network or backend degradations occur.
- Preserve telemetry continuity so downstream incident and cost analysis is accurate.

Scope and audience

- In-scope: SDKs (server and browser-safe shims), service-side adapters, edge proxies, and application integration patterns.
- Out-of-scope: deep server-side model serving internals and on-prem packaging for customers (covered under eng-private-deployments).

Key concepts and terminology

- Request shaping: client-side pre-processing to group, truncate, or transform calls to maximize batching and reduce tokens.
- Token-aware batching: grouping requests by prompt length budget and model variant to form optimal batches.
- Local fallback: strategies executed on the client when Redwood endpoints are degraded (cached responses, smaller model variants, or degraded UX).
- Speculative concurrency: launching multiple candidate requests and using the first acceptable response to reduce tail latency.

Patterns and recipes

1) Token-aware batching (recommended for server SDKs)

- When to use: high QPS, many short prompts (<= 128 tokens), or workloads with many small concurrent requests (chat widgets, autosuggest).
- How it works: group incoming requests into buckets by model, instruction-type, and expected token length. Dispatch a batch when either (a) batch token budget is reached, or (b) max wait (e.g. 15 ms) elapses.

Minimal config (example):

- bucket_key: model_name + instruction_tag
- max_batch_tokens: 16_384
- max_batch_size: 64 requests
- max_wait_ms: 15

Operational notes:

- Choose max_wait_ms to balance throughput and tail latency; 10–25 ms is typical for low-latency services.
- Monitor batch token utilization: aim for 60–85% to avoid wasted compute while keeping SLOs.

2) Prefix/KV caching (client-local & shared caches)

- Use case: assistants and multi-turn chat where many prompts share prefixes or system messages.
- Implementation options:
  - SDK-level in-memory KV cache for a single worker process.
  - Shared Redis/memcached cache for pool-based backends (store serialized prefix KV state).

Cache keys and TTLs:

- key: sha256(model + conversation_id + last_committed_prompt_hash)
- ttl: 5–30 minutes depending on concurrency and conversation stickiness

Data hygiene:

- Ensure cached KV blobs are encrypted at rest when stored in shared caches.
- Invalidate cache on policy or system prompt changes (explicit cache-bust header).

3) Local fallback strategies (graded)

Design fallbacks in tiers from least to most invasive. Choose combinations per route.

- Tier A: Local synthetic reply (best-effort message: "We're having trouble processing your request. Try again in a moment.") – preserves UX but loses LLM fidelity.
- Tier B: Cached golden responses for known prompts (embeddings + retrieval of top-N canonical responses).
- Tier C: Route to smaller/cheaper embedded model (on-device or local microservice) with a post-filter step.
- Tier D: Fallback to read-only user experience (e.g., show last saved state).

Policy and UX guidance:

- Prefer Tier B/C for user-facing critical paths where stale but coherent output is acceptable.
- Always surface that content may be degraded (UI banner or toast).

4) Speculative concurrency (latency-first flows)

- Pattern: for latency-sensitive endpoints, issue two parallel requests: one to the primary production model and another to a smaller low-latency model. Use the first response that passes a basic acceptance filter (non-empty, not obscene, size threshold).
- Cost tradeoff: increases compute cost but can drastically cut P99 latency. Limit speculative requests to important routes (search, assist, autosuggest) and to <5% of total QPS by sampling.

Instrumentation and telemetry (must-haves)

All SDKs and adapters must emit the following telemetry fields on each logical request:

- request_id (UUID)
- client_sdk (name + version)
- model_requested and model_served (string)
- batch_size and batch_token_count (integers)
- shaping_strategy (none | small-batch | full-batch | speculative)
- fallback_action (none | cached | synthetic | reduced_model)
- latency_ms and network_time_ms
- acceptance_result (accepted | rejected_by_filter)

Exporters and traces:

- Span boundaries: client-shaping, outbound-call, cache-lookup, speculative-merge, response-validation.
- Tag the trace with route and SLO tier (e.g., route:search, slo:interactive-100ms).

SLOs and thresholds (suggested)

- P50 latency: 50–100 ms for interactive routes (including client shaping).
- P95 latency: <= 200 ms.
- P99 latency: <= 400 ms (use speculative concurrency to reduce spikes).
- Batch token utilization: target 60–85%.

Quickstart: adding token-aware batching to a Node server SDK

1) Install the batching adapter (example CLI):

npm install @redwood/batch-adapter@latest

2) Minimal adapter config (YAML snippet)

adapter:
  model: redwood-gen-1
  max_batch_tokens: 16384
  max_wait_ms: 15
  acceptance_filter:
    min_tokens: 4

3) Pseudocode (server):

- onIncomingRequest(req):
  - compute bucket_key from model + intent
  - enqueue request into bucket pool
  - when bucket triggers, assemble batch payload, attach request_ids, and call Redwood API
  - fanout responses back to individual waiting requests

Troubleshooting and canonical fixes (top support issues)

Issue: Burst of small requests causing high tail latency and cost
- Symptom: Many 1–2 token prompts under high concurrency, high P99, inefficient GPU utilization.
- Fix: Enable token-aware batching, set min_batch_size or min_batch_tokens to avoid dispatching tiny batches. Add jitter to request arrival times (micro-delay 5–10ms).

Issue: Cache poisoning or stale KV responses
- Symptom: Users receive outdated context or system messages after a rollout.
- Fix: Implement cache-bust on system prompt rollouts; version cache keys using system_prompt_version. Add short TTLs during rollout windows.

Issue: Fallback responses look incoherent or harmful
- Symptom: Local fallback returning content that fails safety checks or confuses users.
- Fix: Add the same safety filter used in production as a lightweight post-filter. For cached golden responses, maintain a small set of QA assertions (regex checks, length bounds, presence of required fields).

Operational playbook: rolling out shaping+fallback

1) Stage in canary environment with 1–2% of traffic routed through shaping adapter. Monitor: batch_utilization, per-request latency, and acceptance rates.
2) Run A/B for fallback UX: compare completion rate and CSAT for degraded flow vs. blocking.
3) Gradually increase to 25% then 100% while validating telemetry correlation.

Production checklist before wide rollout

- SDK emits required telemetry fields and traces.
- Batch adapter has circuit-breaker metrics and configurable thresholds.
- Safety and acceptance filters are present and tested.
- All cache keys are versioned and encrypted for shared caches.
- Rollback plan: disable shaping router and revert to direct calls; ensure canary is small so rollback is immediate.

Ownership and contact points

- Pattern owner: SDK Reliability Team (sre-sdk@redwood.ai)
- Observability: Eng Platform (telemetry@redwood.ai)
- Security review: AppSec (appsec@redwood.ai)

Appendix: example acceptance filter pseudocode

function acceptanceFilter(response) {
  if (!response || response.trim().length === 0) return false;
  if (response.includes('<PROHIBITED_PHRASE>')) return false;
  if (response.split('
').length > 50 && route === 'interactive') return false;
  return true;
}
